ranked_evidence.title: After a decade of teaching college, these are the lessons I wish every freshman already knew - Business Insider
ranked_evidence.snippet: # After a decade of teaching college, these are the lessons I wish every freshman already knew. I am a mom of four, one of whom is dual-enrolled in high school and college courses. I have also taught more than 1,000 college students over the last decade. Here's what I want parents to teach their high school graduates before they head off to college. If your child is going to be absent or is struggling with class material, teach them how to send a respectful e-mail requesting clarification or support. What you should not do is step in and try to talk to teachers on your child's behalf. This is their time to learn, and that includes learning about advocating for themselves. The summer before the fall semester, consider offering to take a self-defense class with your child or sending them to one specifically designed for their age. Now is the time to research the many opportunities their college offers and begin planning for your child to explore them.

ranked_evidence.title: Tinley Park teacher brings lessons of Holocaust home from fellowship: ‘It’s about empathy’ - Chicago Tribune
ranked_evidence.snippet: Daily Southtown |   Tinley Park teacher brings lessons of Holocaust…. # Tinley Park teacher brings lessons of Holocaust home from fellowship: ‘It’s about empathy’. For the past 20 years, Karen Bidus has read “The Diary of Anne Frank” with 6th, 7th and 8th grade students, at Trinity Lutheran School in Tinley Park. “By making it a personal connection, they feel a little bit more in tune with the Holocaust,” said Bidus. Bidus recently had a chance to make make a more personal connection through an Alfred Lerner Fellowship with the Jewish Foundation for the Righteous Summer Institute for Teachers, where Bidus and several dozen other middle and high school teachers, along with educators from across the U.S. and Poland, learned teaching strategies to convey the story of the Holocaust genocide to new generations. “Karen is an engaged and thoughtful teacher who helps her students understand not just the events of the Holocaust, but the human dimension of the history as well — the people involved, and the lessons students can learn and apply to their world today,” said Friedeman.

ranked_evidence.snippet: # Protesters in India reject Modi’s promise of fast-track courts for exam leaks. Opposition groups disrupted parliament for the fourth day this week as protesters from India’s “cockroach” movement continued to demand education reforms. NEW DELHI — Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday that “fast-track” courts would be set up to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks, his first public response after days of youth protests demanding the resignation of the education minister. However, the protesters and opposition parties swiftly rejected Modi’s proposal and insisted that Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan quit first, with opposition groups disrupting parliament for the fourth day this week. Opposition parties have echoed the demands of the youth movement and have disrupted the monsoon session of parliament that began this week. “We have decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks,” he said, adding that those who try to harm the future of young people will not be spared.

ranked_evidence.title: What October 7 Changed for Jews - The Times of Israel
ranked_evidence.snippet: Learning The Lessons Of History. # What October 7 Changed for Jews. On October 7, 2023, the world changed for Jews. The Hamas attack on Israel was the deadliest single-day massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, and the murder, kidnapping and deliberate brutality were horrifying in themselves. Yet for many Jews, the shock did not end with the attack. For many Jews, October 7 became more than a terrorist attack in Israel. It became a psychological turning point that changed how they viewed their security, their place in democratic societies and their confidence in the institutions responsible for protecting them. For generations after the Holocaust, many Jews believed liberal democracies had learned the lessons of history. October 7 did not erase those protections, nor did it make today’s democracies equivalent to Europe in the 1930s and 1940s. What October 7 did, however, was force many Jews to reconsider assumptions they had rarely questioned.
